title: What to do when someone steals your idea: execution beats ideas
summary: Garry Tan explains why good startup ideas are rare and arise from technology, regulation, or macroeconomic shifts, so copycats are inevitable. Ideas only multiply execution; the response is to share loudly, own the problem space, and ship faster than copycats, who can only copy an older version of you.

principles.text: Working startup ideas are rare and unlock via technology, regulation, or macroeconomic shifts, so answer 'why now'.
principles.quote: Good ideas that will actually work are very, very rare, and they come about for just a few reasons. One, technological, two, regulatory, or three, some sort of macroeconomic force that's happening.

principles.text: Because 'why now' forces are shared, others will find your idea too; the idea is just a multiplier on execution.
principles.quote: the idea is only a multiplier on execution. The ideas are out there, everyone can sort of pursue them.

principles.text: Win by execution: build what people need and be chosen over all alternatives.
principles.quote: What's your product like? Is it actually what people need? And do people choose you over all possible alternatives?

principles.text: Don't clam up when facing competition; lean in and be the most associated with the problem space.
principles.quote: You actually have to be so deeply associated with that problem space, and being the best solution for that problem, that you win.

principles.text: A great idea alone isn't enough; success takes manual, relentless work to push it to customers.
principles.quote: a great idea on its own will not be enough. In order to actually take advantage of it, you're going to have to jam it down their throats.

principles.text: Outrun copycats by shipping and going to market faster, so they only copy an older version of you.
principles.quote: even the people who are trying to copy you can only copy the version of you from six or nine months ago.
